exercises.title: Solow convergence speed, derived two ways
exercises.scope: Module 1 §3 (Solow law of motion), §4 (stability and convergence)

sub_moves.label: Anchor
sub_moves.prompt: Recall: in Solow with Cobb-Douglas $f(k) = Bk^\alpha$, capital per worker evolves as $\Delta k_t = sBk_t^\alpha - (n+\delta)k_t$. State the two conditions on $f$ that guarantee a unique stable steady state $k^*$ exists. (One sentence each, no derivation.)
hints: One condition concerns the slope of $f$ as $k \to 0$; another as $k \to \infty$.
These are the Inada conditions.

sub_moves.label: Main proof
sub_moves.prompt: Derive the local convergence speed $\lambda$, defined as the per-period rate at which $\ln k_t - \ln k^*$ contracts. Use the linearization-around-$k^*$ method: log-linearize the Solow equation at $k^*$, identify the coefficient on $\ln k_t - \ln k^*$, and read off $\lambda$. Show every algebraic step.
hints: Take logs of $k_{t+1}/k_t$ and Taylor-expand around $\ln k = \ln k^*$.
At $k^*$, the Solow equation gives $sB(k^*)^{\alpha-1} = n+\delta$ — use this to simplify the coefficient.
The coefficient on $\ln k_t - \ln k^*$ comes out as $-(1-\alpha)(n+\delta)$. Justify the sign before reading $\lambda$.

sub_moves.label: Method variation
sub_moves.prompt: Now derive $\lambda$ a second way. Treat Solow as the nonlinear difference equation $k_{t+1} = \phi(k_t)$, compute $\phi'(k^*)$ explicitly, and connect $\phi'(k^*)$ to your previous $\lambda$. Show the algebra of the connection (not just "they agree").
hints: $\phi(k_t) = k_t + sBk_t^\alpha - (n+\delta)k_t$. Differentiate, then evaluate at $k^*$.
Use the steady-state identity $sB(k^*)^{\alpha-1} = n+\delta$ to simplify $\phi'(k^*)$.

sub_moves.label: Methodology reflection
sub_moves.prompt: Each method makes one move the other doesn't. The linearization is local; the difference-equation method gives a global monotonicity statement under a condition on $\phi'$. State that condition and identify which assumption is load-bearing in each method (2-3 sentences each).

sub_moves.label: Counterfactual
sub_moves.prompt: Suppose $\alpha$ is country-specific: each country $i$ has its own $\alpha_i \in (0,1)$ but shares $s, n, \delta, B$. Does country $i$'s convergence speed depend only on $\alpha_i$, or do cross-country spillovers enter? Argue from the step of your main proof that does (or doesn't) get contaminated. Rapid prose, no full re-derivation.

exercises.solution:
Anchor

The two conditions are the Inada conditions: $\lim_{k\to 0} f'(k) = \infty$ (so investment dominates depreciation near zero, forcing $k$ to grow) and $\lim_{k\to\infty} f'(k) = 0$ (so eventually depreciation dominates, forcing $k$ to fall). Together with concavity, these guarantee a unique interior crossing of $sf(k)$ and $(n+\delta)k$.

Main proof — linearization

Step 1 Start from $k_{t+1} = k_t + sBk_t^\alpha - (n+\delta)k_t$. Take logs of both sides — but logs don't distribute over sums, so instead define $\tilde k_t = \ln k_t$ and write $k_t = e^{\tilde k_t}$.
Step 2 Equivalently, divide by $k_t$: $k_{t+1}/k_t = 1 + sBk_t^{\alpha-1} - (n+\delta)$. Take logs: $\ln(k_{t+1}/k_t) = \ln[1 + sBk_t^{\alpha-1} - (n+\delta)]$.
Step 3 First-order Taylor around $k_t = k^*$ (where the bracket equals 1): $\ln(k_{t+1}/k_t) \approx sBk_t^{\alpha-1} - (n+\delta)$.
Step 4 Now linearize $sBk_t^{\alpha-1}$ around $k^*$. Use $k_t = k^* + (k_t - k^*) \approx k^*(1 + \delta_t)$ where $\delta_t = (k_t - k^*)/k^*$. Then $k_t^{\alpha-1} \approx (k^*)^{\alpha-1}(1 + (\alpha-1)\delta_t)$.
Step 5 Substituting and using the steady-state identity $sB(k^*)^{\alpha-1} = n+\delta$ gives $\ln(k_{t+1}/k_t) \approx (n+\delta)(\alpha - 1)(\tilde k_t - \tilde k^*)$.
Step 6 Since $\ln(k_{t+1}/k_t) = \tilde k_{t+1} - \tilde k_t$, we get $\tilde k_{t+1} - \tilde k_t = -(1-\alpha)(n+\delta)(\tilde k_t - \tilde k^*)$, i.e. $(\tilde k_{t+1} - \tilde k^*) = [1 - (1-\alpha)(n+\delta)](\tilde k_t - \tilde k^*)$.
Convergence speed (linearization): $\lambda = (1-\alpha)(n+\delta)$.

Method variation — difference equation

Step 1 $\phi(k_t) = k_t + sBk_t^\alpha - (n+\delta)k_t$, so $\phi'(k_t) = 1 + \alpha sBk_t^{\alpha-1} - (n+\delta)$.
Step 2 At $k^*$: $sB(k^*)^{\alpha-1} = n+\delta$, hence $\alpha sB(k^*)^{\alpha-1} = \alpha(n+\delta)$.
Step 3 Substituting: $\phi'(k^*) = 1 + \alpha(n+\delta) - (n+\delta) = 1 - (1-\alpha)(n+\delta)$.
Step 4 Connection: the linearized recursion $(\tilde k_{t+1} - \tilde k^*) = [1 - (1-\alpha)(n+\delta)](\tilde k_t - \tilde k^*)$ has the SAME coefficient $\phi'(k^*)$ that we just derived. So $\lambda = 1 - \phi'(k^*) = (1-\alpha)(n+\delta)$.
Same $\lambda$, second route: $1 - \phi'(k^*) = (1-\alpha)(n+\delta)$.

Methodology reflection

Linearization assumes you're in a neighborhood of $k^*$ where the Taylor expansion is accurate — the result is a strictly local statement about the contraction rate near the steady state. The difference-equation method, by contrast, exploits monotonicity globally: $\phi$ is monotone-increasing and concave, so iterating $\phi$ from any positive starting point produces a monotone sequence; the load-bearing condition for convergence is $|\phi'(k^*)| < 1$, which here equals $|1 - (1-\alpha)(n+\delta)| < 1$ — guaranteed for any $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and any reasonable $n+\delta < 1$.

Counterfactual: country-specific $\alpha_i$

Inspect the load-bearing step: $\lambda = (1-\alpha)(n+\delta)$. The only parameters that enter are local — $\alpha_i$, $n$, $\delta$. There is no term that depends on other countries' parameters. So in a basic closed-economy Solow framework with country-specific $\alpha_i$ but shared $(s, n, \delta)$, each country's convergence speed depends ONLY on its own $\alpha_i$. Cross-country spillovers would only enter if capital mobility were added (open economy, where $\bar r$ is set by world markets) — that's a Module 2 conversation, not a Module 1 closed-economy one.

exercises.title: Cobb-Douglas factor shares: prove and break
exercises.scope: Module 1 §2 (production function), §3 (factor prices and Euler theorem)

sub_moves.label: Main proof
sub_moves.prompt: Prove that in a Cobb-Douglas economy $Y = BK^\alpha L^{1-\alpha}$ under perfect competition, the capital income share $rK/Y$ is exactly $\alpha$ — independent of $K$, $L$, $B$, and time. Start from the firm's profit-max FOCs. State explicitly which step gives "share = exponent" and which step gives "share is constant".
hints: Two FOCs: $r = \partial Y / \partial K$ and $w = \partial Y / \partial L$.
Compute $\partial Y / \partial K$ and simplify using $Y = BK^\alpha L^{1-\alpha}$.
$rK = \alpha Y$ follows in one line. The "share is constant" part comes from $K$ and $L$ canceling.

sub_moves.label: Falsification probe
sub_moves.prompt:
Consider CES production $Y = B[\alpha K^\rho + (1-\alpha) L^\rho]^{1/\rho}$ with $\rho < 1, \rho \ne 0$. The elasticity of substitution is $\sigma = 1/(1-\rho)$; Cobb-Douglas is the limit $\rho \to 0$ (so $\sigma = 1$).

  1. Derive $rK/Y$ in the CES case. Show every algebraic step.
  2. Show that $rK/Y$ is not constant in $K/L$ when $\rho \ne 0$. Identify, as a function of $\rho$, whether $rK/Y$ rises or falls when $K/L$ rises.
  3. Identify the single mathematical fact about Cobb-Douglas that breaks under CES — the one that made the share trivially constant in the Cobb-Douglas case.
hints: Compute $\partial Y / \partial K$ via the chain rule. The inner derivative is $\alpha \rho K^{\rho-1}$.
$rK/Y$ simplifies to $\alpha K^\rho / [\alpha K^\rho + (1-\alpha)L^\rho]$. Now divide top and bottom by $L^\rho$ — note what depends on $K/L$.

The Cobb-Douglas fact that breaks: in CD, $rK/Y = \alpha K \cdot Y/K \cdot 1/Y = \alpha$ trivially because the exponent on $K$ in $Y$ equals $\alpha$. In CES, $K$ enters non-trivially through a bracketed term.

sub_moves.label: Counterfactual
sub_moves.prompt:
Recent data show the labor share declining in advanced economies since around 2000, while $K/L$ has risen.

  1. Which sign of $\rho$ in CES production is consistent with this empirical pattern?
  2. In terms of $\sigma$, is the elasticity of substitution greater than 1 or less than 1?
  3. Kaldor's "constant labor share" fact is one of his five stylized facts. If data contradicts it, does Cobb-Douglas remain a usable approximation, or does the constancy become a load-bearing assumption that distorts model predictions about distribution? (Rapid prose.)

exercises.solution:
Main proof

(Full derivation goes here. Approx. 400 words. Show FOC computation, simplification, and the cancellation step that makes the share constant.)

Cobb-Douglas capital share: $rK/Y = \alpha$, exactly.

Falsification probe

(CES derivation here. Approx. 500 words. Show that $rK/Y = \alpha (K/L)^\rho / [\alpha (K/L)^\rho + (1-\alpha)]$, which DOES depend on $K/L$ for $\rho \ne 0$.)

CES capital share: $rK/Y = \dfrac{\alpha (K/L)^\rho}{\alpha (K/L)^\rho + (1-\alpha)}$ — varies with $K/L$.

Counterfactual

(~300 words: $\rho > 0$, $\sigma > 1$, Cobb-Douglas becomes a load-bearing assumption about distribution, etc.)

exercises.title: Golden Rule via envelope theorem

sub_moves.label: Main proof
sub_moves.prompt: Derive the Golden Rule saving rate $s^{**}$ that maximizes steady-state consumption per worker $c^*(s)$ in basic Solow with Cobb-Douglas. Use the envelope theorem: write $c^*(s) = (1-s) y^*(s)$, differentiate with respect to $s$, and use the steady-state condition to simplify the derivative of $y^*$.
hints: $y^*(s) = B[s/(n+\delta)]^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)}$. Compute $dy^*/ds$.
Or: use $sBk^{*\alpha} = (n+\delta)k^*$ implicitly and differentiate.

sub_moves.label: Method variation
sub_moves.prompt: Now derive $s^{**} = \alpha$ a second way: use the modified Golden Rule condition $\text{MPK} = n + \delta$ at the optimum. Show that $\text{MPK} = \alpha(n+\delta)/s$ at any steady state, and combine to get $s^{**} = \alpha$.
hints: Steady-state $r = \alpha B (k^*)^{\alpha-1}$. Use $sB(k^*)^{\alpha-1} = n+\delta$.
$\text{MPK}_{\text{at GR}} = n+\delta$, so $\alpha (n+\delta)/s = n+\delta \Rightarrow s = \alpha$.

sub_moves.label: Counterfactual
sub_moves.prompt: What is the Golden Rule under labor-augmenting technology growth $g$? Sketch the change to the FOC and to $s^{**}$. (Rapid; no full derivation.)

exercises.solution:
Main proof

(~500 words: derive $s^{**} = \alpha$ via envelope theorem on $c^*(s) = (1-s)y^*(s)$.)

Golden Rule: $s^{**} = \alpha$.

Method variation

(~400 words: derive same result from MPK = n+δ condition.)

Counterfactual

(~300 words: with $g > 0$, the condition becomes MPK = $n + \delta + g$, but $s^{**} = \alpha$ still holds because both sides scale together.)

exercises.title: Numeric inversion: recover α from observed savings and rental rate

figure.caption: Steady state at the intersection of $sf(k)$ and $(n+\delta)k$.

sub_moves.label: Computation
sub_moves.prompt: Suppose the observed long-run saving rate is $s = 0.25$, observed depreciation plus population growth is $n+\delta = 0.05$, and observed steady-state rental rate is $r^* = 0.05$. Under basic Solow with Cobb-Douglas, what value of $\alpha$ is consistent with these observations? Show the inversion algebra (no calculator-style "plug in formula and compute").
hints: At the steady state: $r^* = \alpha(n+\delta)/s$. Solve for $\alpha$.
$\alpha = r^* \cdot s / (n+\delta)$. Substitute the observed values.

sub_moves.label: Reflection
sub_moves.prompt: The value of $\alpha$ you just recovered should be compared against the textbook estimate $\alpha \approx 1/3$ (capital share in national accounts). Is the recovered value consistent? If not, what does that suggest about the model — is it the Cobb-Douglas assumption that fails, the closed-economy assumption, or the perfect-competition assumption?

sub_moves.label: Counterfactual
sub_moves.prompt: If the world interest rate were to drop from $\bar r = 0.05$ to $\bar r = 0.03$ in an open economy, what would happen to the steady-state $k^*$? Show that the answer depends only on the ratio of rates and on $\alpha$, not on $B$. Rapid algebra.
hints: In open economy: $k^* = (\alpha B / \bar r)^{1/(1-\alpha)}$. Take the ratio of old to new $k^*$.

exercises.solution:
Computation

Step 1 Steady-state rental rate: $r^* = \alpha B (k^*)^{\alpha - 1}$. Combine with $sB(k^*)^{\alpha-1} = n+\delta$ to eliminate $B(k^*)^{\alpha-1}$:
Step 2 $B(k^*)^{\alpha-1} = (n+\delta)/s$, hence $r^* = \alpha (n+\delta)/s$.
Step 3 Invert: $\alpha = r^* \cdot s / (n+\delta) = 0.05 \cdot 0.25 / 0.05 = 0.25$.
Recovered $\alpha$: $0.25$.

Reflection

0.25 is lower than the textbook $\alpha \approx 1/3$. Possible explanations: (a) Cobb-Douglas may be wrong (CES with $\sigma < 1$ could give a lower implied $\alpha$); (b) markup over marginal cost in imperfect competition drives a wedge between MPK and observed $r^*$; (c) the closed-economy assumption fails — if capital flows internationally, the observed $r^*$ is not the local MPK. Each fits different empirical literatures.

Counterfactual

In open economy $k^* = (\alpha B / \bar r)^{1/(1-\alpha)}$. So $k^*_{\text{new}} / k^*_{\text{old}} = (\bar r_{\text{old}} / \bar r_{\text{new}})^{1/(1-\alpha)} = (0.05/0.03)^{1/0.75} \approx 1.93$. $B$ cancels because it appears identically in both terms. Capital nearly doubles when the world rate falls by 40%.

exercises.title: Cross-module bridge: Euler identity → open-economy MPK pinning
exercises.scope: Module 1 §3 (Euler theorem) used to derive a Module 2 (open economy) result. Cross-module by design.

sub_moves.label: Anchor
sub_moves.prompt: From Module 1, restated: Euler's theorem for constant-returns Cobb-Douglas gives the factor-share identity $rK + wL = Y$ with $rK/Y = \alpha$, $wL/Y = 1-\alpha$. Confirm in one line that this identity holds in any closed-or-open economy where production is Cobb-Douglas with $\alpha + (1-\alpha) = 1$.

sub_moves.label: Main proof
sub_moves.prompt: In the open economy, the world interest rate $\bar r$ is exogenous, so the firm's FOC $r = \bar r$ pins down $K/L$. Derive the open-economy steady-state $k^*_{\text{open}} = (\alpha B / \bar r)^{1/(1-\alpha)}$. Do this twice: first from the FOC $r = \alpha B (K/L)^{\alpha-1}$, then from the factor-share identity $rK/Y = \alpha$ with $r = \bar r$. Show that both routes give the same $k^*_{\text{open}}$.
hints: Route 1: set $\bar r = \alpha B k^{\alpha-1}$ and isolate $k$.
Route 2: $\alpha = \bar r K/Y$. Substitute $Y = BK^\alpha L^{1-\alpha}$, simplify.

sub_moves.label: Methodology reflection
sub_moves.prompt: The two routes differ in which equation does the work: route 1 leans on the firm FOC; route 2 leans on the accounting identity that follows from Euler's theorem. Are these two routes equivalent in EVERY production function, or specifically in Cobb-Douglas? (One sentence answer with one-sentence justification.)

exercises.solution:
Anchor

Cobb-Douglas $Y = BK^\alpha L^{1-\alpha}$ is homogeneous of degree 1: $Y(\lambda K, \lambda L) = \lambda Y(K, L)$. Euler's theorem applies, giving $F_K K + F_L L = Y$. The shares $F_K K/Y$ and $F_L L/Y$ are the exponents $\alpha$ and $1-\alpha$.

Main proof — route 1 (firm FOC)

Step 1 $\bar r = \alpha B K^{\alpha-1} L^{1-\alpha} = \alpha B (K/L)^{\alpha-1}$.
Step 2 Isolate $(K/L)^{\alpha-1} = \bar r / (\alpha B)$. Raise to $1/(\alpha-1) = -1/(1-\alpha)$.
Step 3 $k^*_{\text{open}} = (\alpha B / \bar r)^{1/(1-\alpha)}$.

Main proof — route 2 (Euler factor share)

Step 1 $\alpha = \bar r K / Y$, hence $\bar r = \alpha Y/K$.
Step 2 Substitute $Y = BK^\alpha L^{1-\alpha}$: $\bar r = \alpha B K^{\alpha-1} L^{1-\alpha} = \alpha B (K/L)^{\alpha-1}$.
Step 3 Same equation as route 1, step 1. Isolating $k$ gives the same result.
Open-economy capital intensity: $k^*_{\text{open}} = (\alpha B / \bar r)^{1/(1-\alpha)}$.

Methodology reflection

The two routes are equivalent specifically in Cobb-Douglas because there the share IS the exponent. In CES (where $rK/Y \ne \alpha$), the factor-share equation no longer reads $\bar r = \alpha Y/K$, so route 2 would need to be redone with the CES share expression. Route 1 (firm FOC) generalizes; route 2 (share identity) is Cobb-Douglas-specific.
